title: Vesper and the Prom
premise: Paloma Ashgrove has spent four years perfecting the art of being unseen: she cooks, she cleans, she covers for her mother's night shifts at the hospital, and she never, ever lets the school counselor look too closely at home. But senior English hands her an essay prompt she can't dodge—'Describe a moment you chose to be honest, and what it cost you'—and her draft, written at 2 a.m. in the kitchen, accidentally gets submitted in the college application packet her counselor mails early. When her essay is read aloud at the winter assembly as a model of 'authentic voice,' Paloma's carefully sealed life cracks open in front of the whole school, including Theo Marchetti, the boy who's been quietly leaving granola bars in her locker since October. As her mother's hours are cut and her younger sister acts out the family's shame at school, Paloma must choose between protecting the secret that has kept her family fed and claiming a future that requires her to be seen. On the night of the winter formal she swore she'd never attend, she walks in alone, reads the true ending of her essay over the gym speakers, and discovers that belonging was never something she could earn by disappearing—it was waiting for her the whole time she was hiding.
about_author: A. M. Vasquez is a former high school English teacher who spent a decade collecting the essays students wrote when they thought no one was reading. They write young adult novels from a small apartment full of houseplants and other people's unsent letters.

chapters.title: The Prompt Nobody Can Skip
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. We meet the Ashgrove household at 5:47 a.m.—toast stretched four ways, seven-year-old Milo's shoelaces, sixteen-year-old Juniper's slammed door—before Paloma slips into school and becomes invisible. English teacher Ms. Okafor assigns the honesty essay, and Paloma plans to write safe fiction. But at 2 a.m., alone in the kitchen, the truth pours out of her. Beat: the quiet ache of a girl who has mistaken duty for identity.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with a shift to Theo's at the midpoint. The counselor's early-deadline mix-up means Paloma's raw 2 a.m. draft is read at the winter assembly as an exemplar essay. The gym goes silent as her family's reality unfolds sentence by sentence. Theo, the boy behind the locker granola bars, is the only one who doesn't look away. Juniper storms out; Mom finds out her secret is public. Beat: exposure as both catastrophe and strange relief.

chapters.title: What the Labels Cost
chapters.summary: Alternating Paloma and Juniper POV. The fallout: classmates' pity, Mom's fury and exhaustion, a visit from a school social worker that threatens the fragile system holding the family together. Juniper acts out to force the family's shame into the open, and Paloma realizes her invisibility was never protection—it was a cage she built for everyone. Theo asks her to the formal; she says no. Beat: the breaking point, where survival and love collide.

chapters.title: The Last Game
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Mom's shift ends early; for the first time, the Ashgroves face their life together instead of around each other. Paloma rewrites her essay with the real ending—then, at the winter formal she swore off, she takes the microphone during the last slow song and reads it aloud, not as confession but as claim. Theo finds her under the paper stars; Juniper saves her a seat. Beat: belonging chosen, not earned—the labels come off, and she is still here.
